signals.title: Creativity in the Age of AI
signals.description: A few years before they closed, Space10 made a short film called Creativity in the Age of AI . It runs through the history of creative tools and asks what AI changes about the act of making. I keep coming back to this film these days. So let’s explore the studio behind it and explain how they pushed the boundaries of creativity in the age of AI. Located in Copenhagen’s Meatpacking District, the SPACE10 office is where the community, ideas, and explorations intersected. A studio that built by asking better questions Space10 was IKEA’s research and design lab in Copenhagen. It started in 2014, out of a project between IKEA and a Danish design collective called ArtRebels who had designed a furniture line for the retailer. When then-CEO Torbjörn Lööf called them in for a follow-up, they could have proposed another product line. But they proposed something else, as rebels do. Instead of just creating a better future for IKEA, our starting point was asking how IKEA could help create a better future for the world,” Simon Caspersen told Fast Company in 2015 . “Let’s get rid of the whole client-agency model, have IKEA pay the basic fees and costs of running a space, and then devote ourselves to looking 10 or 20 years down the pipeline. That arrangement is what made the work possible. A small team with a long horizon, free of campaigns and quarterly deliverables, working on questions that took years to answer. So they took strange ones. What if hotdogs had no meat. What if homes shipped flat and assembled in a day. What if a village block was the unit of urban design instead of the apartment. The output looked like prototypes and films and exhibitions. The real product was a way of thinking about the future that didn’t sound like a press release. How can AI assist designers to make more sustainable products using abundant local materials? Products of Place: Localised Design with AI I was envy of it. I still am to be honest. As a solo designer, you read about a place like that and you want to be in the room with curious people working on real stuff, tinkering at the highest level. Sadly they closed shop in 2023. But the highlights are still up. Go get lost in them. They are very inspiring projects. How they used AI Most teams now use AI to ship faster. Space10 used it to think further. They used AI to shorten the distance between an idea and a prototype they could look at and discuss about. The argument is still human. The making is partly machine. An emerging type of collaboration. DOC put the question well in their piece on the studio: When we consider the utility of AI in creativity as a feature that helps us create meaning instead of consuming content, it provides a means for us to frame how we build tools that act as collaborative partners in creative work and stimulate our creative action. So, when building creative tools with this in mind, what should the actual interaction design between humans and AI look like? — Collected Consciousness, DOC That’s the part most product teams skip. The question we should be asking is what the interaction looks like when a person and a model are working on the same thing at the same time. Space10 treated that as a design problem. The result is a studio that used AI to go deeper into questions about food, shelter, cities, and loneliness. They handed over some of the iteration and kept the question. Bee Home is a free and open-sourced design, pioneering a new era of democratic design for IKEA. The fears are old We’ve been here before. People were hostile to the camera. They were hostile to the automobile, to recorded music, to the personal computer. Painters thought photography would end painting. It ended a particular kind of portrait commission and freed painting to do something else. The fears around AI with those. Some of it is about jobs. Some is about craft. Some is about consent. Artists’ work became training data without their permission. Styles that took twenty years to develop are a prompt away. That’s a property question we still haven’t answered. The rest of the resistance follows the usual shape. A new tool changes who gets to make things, and the speed it brings starts to feel like the point. I wrote about this in Efficiency over Craftsmanship : the more design optimizes for output, the more the work drifts toward the average. AI is the strongest accelerant we’ve had. The risk is the same as before. We mistake faster for better, ship more of the average, and stop noticing what’s missing. Space10’s film tells a different use of the same tool: keep the craft, let the machine carry some of the iteration. The value of most essays we write over a lifetime sits in the effort of writing them. The thinking happens in the friction. If we hand the friction to a model, we get the essay and lose the thinking. If we hand the iteration to a model and keep the question, we get more thinking, faster. Space10’s film is an argument for the second one. Made by a team that built that way for nine years before it closed. Worth watching, and worth borrowing from. — Thanks for reading. Always good to hear what you think. Comments open. The Urban Village Project : a proposal for shared, modular living at the block scale, with EFFEKT Architects. SolarVille : a miniature neighborhood prototype running on solar microgrids and peer-to-peer energy trading. Everyday Experiments : short films exploring how spatial computing and AI could reshape the home. Bee Home : open-source, downloadable beehive designs. signals.title: #299 | finalmente podemos medir as redes sociais no Google
signals.description: Oi, gente 👋 Essa semana eu fiquei com uma sensação muito clara: trabalhar com redes sociais é cada vez menos para amadores - o fazedor de post, sabe? Novas camadas foram sendo adicionadas: busca, IA, distribuição mais complexa, novas métricas, novas análises, novas possibilidades. As notícias desta edição reforçam essa ideia. TL;DR Resumo do resumo das principais notícias da semana 🧠 Google Search Console agora mostra dados das redes sociais: pela primeira vez, profissionais de social media conseguem medir como seus conteúdos circulam na Busca do Google. 🧠 Instagram pode cobrar pelo uso de IA: Mosseri confirmou que recursos avançados devem ganhar uma versão paga. 🧠 TikTok aperta o cerco ao spam de IA: plataforma passa a mirar contas que publicam conteúdo sintético em massa. 🧠 Europa questiona o “design viciante” da Meta: Facebook e Instagram podem ser obrigados a rever recursos como rolagem infinita, autoplay e notificações. 🧠 IA ganha espaço na escolha de marcas: novas pesquisas mostram que consumidores estão usando cada vez mais IA para pesquisar produtos e decidir o que comprar. MANDA NEWS Links e novidades mais relevantes da semana. Isso é GIGANTE: o Google Search Console agora mostra como posts do Instagram, TikTok, X e YouTube performam na Busca e no Discover. O que muda no trabalho de social media com os novos dados do Google Search Console? Spoilier: muda tudo. Rosto sorridente rachado, picles e farol: conheça os novos emojis do iPhone 2027. Eu amo. Cada novo emoji abre novas possibilidades de comunicação pra gente. Essa semana rolou um bafafá sobre a fonte anti-IA, que só os humanos conseguem ler . Mas já foi testado e comprovado que as IAs conseguem ler, sim. Leia a thread abaixo do comentário do usuário SeriouslyYoutube. Autoridades britânicas propõem o apagão das redes sociais para adolescentes durante a noite. União Europeia exige que Meta mude o ‘design viciante’ do Facebook e do Instagram e é importante a gente acompanhar o caso. 🧠 Estão questionando diretamente o modelo que sustenta as principais métricas das redes sociais. Caso a Meta seja obrigada a criar pausas reais ou mudar seus sistemas de recomendação, alcance, retenção e comportamento de consumo devem mudar também. MANDA DADOS McKinsey analisa a jornada de consumo da Gen Z: As redes sociais são a fonte mais importante para a Gen Z tanto na descoberta de marcas quanto na compra. Influenciadores viraram fonte de informação sobre saúde. Pew analisa como jovens consomem conteúdo de saúde . Perigoso demais, vixe. Alô Mari Kruguer! Podcast em áudio e vídeo gera comportamentos diferentes. Nielsen compara quem escuta e quem assiste a podcasts . Ipsos investiga o uso de IA nas compras . Ela já já participa da consideração, mas ainda não conquistou confiança suficiente para assumir a decisão. BCG mede a influência da IA sobre as decisões. O número de pessoas que usa a ferramenta pra pesquisas marcas e serviços segue crescendo. 🧠 O marketing passa a trabalhar com dois caminhos de influência: um voltado à atenção humana e outro à avaliação feita por sistemas. trabalho cada vez mais complexo, e cada vez menos amador Artigo: Evite que a IA prejudique sua marc a . Harvard Business Review alerta para o desgaste acumulado pela automação Dados próprios aumentam as chances de citação pela IA. A Similarweb defende que levantamentos, pesquisas e números exclusivos dão aos sistemas de IA um motivo concreto para citar a fonte original. 🧠 Dados internos podem virar conteúdo de autoridade. Mas precisam ser publicados com número, metodologia, amostra, período e fonte claramente visíveis, e não enterrados em um PDF impossível de encontrar. MANDA DICAS Hootsuite atualiza guia de mensuração de ROI nas redes sociais. Sprout Social ensina a avaliar se vale entrar no Bluesky e como criar estratégias pra lá. Estratégia de marketing com micro-influenciadore s: como encontrar, fazer parceria e medir pequenos criadores, via Later. Como as principais marcas estão ativando criadores no TikTok para impulsionar resultados reais de negócios, via Later. Agora, as novidades de cada rede. INSTAGRAM Adam Mosseri diz que creators humanos ficarão mais valiosos com a enxurrada de IA. Ele argumentou que, quanto mais conteúdo sintético circular, maior será o valor de perspectivas humanas. Instagram prepara cobrança pelo uso de I A. Mosseri confirmou que futuras ferramentas de IA do Instagram deverão ter limites de uso gratuito e opções pagas. Instagram Reels adiciona mais traduções de IA em japonês, coreano, francês, alemão e italiano Instagram começa a alertar responsáveis sobre conversas preocupantes com a Meta AI FACEBOOK/META Recuou : Dois dias depois de liberar um recurso que permitia citar contas públicas do Instagram e usar seus conteúdos em imagens geradas por IA, a Meta tirou a função do ar. Meta adiciona novas métricas para acompanhar o desempenho dos chatbots THREADS O Threads agora permite curtidas privadas , onde apenas você e a pessoa que postou poderão ver que você curtiu a postagem dela. Threads adiciona tags para posts da comunidade TELEGRAM Adorei! O Telegram lançou um e ditor para textos com até 32.768 caracteres , títulos, tabelas, listas, imagens e vídeos incorporados. A atualização também permite reunir diferentes canais, grupos e bots dentro de uma mesma Comunidade. LINKED IN O LinkedIn compartihou dicas para creators e marcas: Publique de 2 a 3 vezes por semana Comece pela informação mais importante Estruture o post como pergunta e resposta Mantenha os posts entre 200 e 300 palavras Compartilhe insights atuais, perguntas que estimulem conversas ou resuma conteúdos mais longos Publique uma combinação de posts e artigos Como o algoritmo do LinkedIn funciona em 2026 , via Hootsuite. TIKTOK Madonna bate recorde de audiência em live no TikTok. Foram mais de 2,1 milhões de espectadores simultâneos. TikTok aperta o cerco ao spam de IA. Empresa vai testar sistemas para identificar contas dedicadas a publicar grandes volumes de conteúdo gerado por IA, e lança medidas de alfabetização . Vídeos gerados por IA estão sendo usados em escala para vender produtos no TikTok Shop, inclusive com avatares fazendo demonstrações (que nunca aconteceram, né?). Algumas marcas já começaram a proibir esse tipo de conteúdo. Vendedores do TikTok Shop no Reino Unido ganharam um painel mais detalhado para entender como os produtos são descobertos. 🧠 Estar por dentro dos lançamentos das ferramentas é importante, mesmo quando não estão liberadas por aqui ainda. É uma forma de se preparar para as novidades que estão chegando. YOUTUBE Um novo material do YouTube mostra como creators ajudam marcas e ligas a ocupar os momentos antes e depois das partidas Como converter visualizações do YouTube Shorts em crescimento de canais longos. Artigo oficial da plataforma. X O X alterou seu sistema de recomendação para valorizar mais publicações de contas que seguem o usuário e são seguidas por ele. A proposta é aumentar a presença de relações reais e reduzir interações excessivamente hostis entre desconhecidos. Que evolução! X alterou também seu sistema para de tectar contas adeptas do engagement bait . Isso é interessante: X transforma prova social em anúncio . O X começou a integrar insi ghts produzidos pelo Grok ao gerenciador de anúncios. GOOGLE Em comemoração aos 25 anos do Google Imagens, empresa apresenta interface no estilo Pinterest . A experiência, inicialmente disponível nos Estados Unidos, também permite salvar imagens em coleções. O Google começou a conectar o Modo IA da Busca a serviços externos. Usuários poderão realizar ações em aplicativos como Canva, Instacart e YouTube Music sem sair da experiência de busca. Quando as marcas usam ferramentas de inteligência artificial generativa em suas promoções, o SynthID do Google detectará e rotulará automaticamente o conteúdo. NOS VEMOS PESSOALMENTE? Estou muito honrada em fazer parte do line-up incrível do melhor evento de marketing digital do Brasil, que conta com a curadoria de ninguém menos que o Rafael Rez. Em agosto, vou falar pela primeira vez sobre um tema que venho desenvolvendo há meses: o impacto estratégico da IA no trabalho com redes sociais. Thinker tem 10% de desconto nos ingressos Conteúdo e VIP com o cupom ANARP10 . Saiba mais e participe BEIJO ESPECIAL PARA NOSSOS APOIADORES Beijo especial aos nossos apoiadores: Daniely Favilla da Silva, Júlia Weibert, Andressa Stevanelli da Silva, Fernanda de azevedo, Dâmaris Letícia Kellner, Alexsandro de Lima Silva, Weslley Alberto da Silva Santana, Solange Neiva, Gabriel Henrique Dias Da Silva, Mariana Paz, Isabela Vanuchi, Maria Silva, Mariana Paz, Francielly Aparecida Dos Santos Freitas, Juliana Vilela de Oliveira Rocha, Luiza Caroline, Manoela Da Silva Castro, Brenda Moreira Silva, Fábio Sina, Daiara Geremia Soares, Daiara Geremia Soares, Thais Moreira Rodrigues, Felipe Barbosa Santos, Andrea Gasques, Tathi Marceli, Gedeon Ferreira Lima, Krízia de Meneses Escórcio, Izadora Szpisjak, Gabriela d'Ávila, Fernanda de azevedo, Jéssica Akemi Moreira, Lana Catharine Silva Queiroz, Felipe Barbosa Santos, Vitória Maria, Gabriela Araújo, Ana Carolina Oliveira, Carolina Mello, Fabiana Pereira, Renata Brito, Lorrayne Cristina Alves da Silva, Karla Nogueira, Julho Medeiros, July Medeiros, Fabiana Pereira, Vinicius Nunes, Claudia Brito, Ana Flaira Palmeira Lima, Maria Eduarda, Luane Abatti, Paula Oliveira, Raphaela Barreto Melnik, Alessandra Martins Siqueira, Raphaela Barreto, Stephanie Kern, Gustavo Reis, Beatriz de la Bandeira, Jessica Galvão, Maira Masiero e Arianny Dias. So they took strange ones. What if hotdogs had no meat. What if homes shipped flat and assembled in a day. What if a village block was the unit of urban design instead of the apartment. The output looked like prototypes and films and exhibitions. The real product was a way of thinking about the future that didn’t sound like a press release. How can AI assist designers to make more sustainable products using abundant local materials? Products of Place: Localised Design with AI I was envy of it. I still am to be honest. As a solo designer, you read about a place like that and you want to be in the room with curious people working on real stuff, tinkering at the highest level. Sadly they closed shop in 2023. But the highlights are still up. Go get lost in them. They are very inspiring projects. How they used AI Most teams now use AI to ship faster. Space10 used it to think further. They used AI to shorten the distance between an idea and a prototype they could look at and discuss about. The argument is still human. The making is partly machine. An emerging type of collaboration. DOC put the question well in their piece on the studio: When we consider the utility of AI in creativity as a feature that helps us create meaning instead of consuming content, it provides a means for us to frame how we build tools that act as collaborative partners in creative work and stimulate our creative action. So, when building creative tools with this in mind, what should the actual interaction design between humans and AI look like? — Collected Consciousness, DOC That’s the part most product teams skip. The question we should be asking is what the interaction looks like when a person and a model are working on the same thing at the same time. Space10 treated that as a design problem. The result is a studio that used AI to go deeper into questions about food, shelter, cities, and loneliness. They handed over some of the iteration and kept the question. Bee Home is a free and open-sourced design, pioneering a new era of democratic design for IKEA. The fears are old We’ve been here before. People were hostile to the camera. They were hostile to the automobile, to recorded music, to the personal computer. Painters thought photography would end painting. It ended a particular kind of portrait commission and freed painting to do something else. The fears around AI with those. Some of it is about jobs. Some is about craft. Some is about consent. Artists’ work became training data without their permission. Styles that took twenty years to develop are a prompt away. That’s a property question we still haven’t answered. The rest of the resistance follows the usual shape. A new tool changes who gets to make things, and the speed it brings starts to feel like the point. I wrote about this in Efficiency over Craftsmanship : the more design optimizes for output, the more the work drifts toward the average. AI is the strongest accelerant we’ve had. The risk is the same as before. We mistake faster for better, ship more of the average, and stop noticing what’s missing. Space10’s film tells a different use of the same tool: keep the craft, let the machine carry some of the iteration. The value of most essays we write over a lifetime sits in the effort of writing them. The thinking happens in the friction. If we hand the friction to a model, we get the essay and lose the thinking. If we hand the iteration to a model and keep the question, we get more thinking, faster. Space10’s film is an argument for the second one. Made by a team that built that way for nine years before it closed. Worth watching, and worth borrowing from. — Thanks for reading. Always good to hear what you think. Comments open. SolarVille : a miniature neighborhood prototype running on solar microgrids and peer-to-peer energy trading. visualFeast.title: Designer Portraits: Susan Kare ⌘ The woman who gave the computer a face
visualFeast.description: Good design is not about what medium you are working in. It’s about thinking hard about what you want to do and what you have to work with before you start. — SK Susan Kare joined Apple in 1982 as the sole creator of screen graphics in the Macintosh group. As the designer “ who gave the Macintosh a smile ” she is best known for developing the distinctive icons, typefaces, and other pixel elements that gave the Macintosh its characteristic look and feel. A sculptor picks up graph paper In 1982, Susan Kare was living in the Bay Area, welding a life-size razorback hog for a museum in Hot Springs, Arkansas. Her father, Morley Richard Kare, had founded the Monell Chemical Senses Center in Philadelphia, spending his career studying taste and smell. His daughter had a PhD from NYU, a background in sculpture and fine art, and zero experience with computers. Then Andy Hertzfeld called. Hertzfeld and Kare had known each other since they were fourteen, classmates at Harriton High School outside Philadelphia. He was now the lead software architect on a secret project at Apple: the Macintosh. He needed someone to design the icons and typefaces for its screen. He told her if she got some graph paper, she could make small images. Kare went to the University Art supply store in Palo Alto and bought a $2.50 sketchbook. That sketchbook now sits in the Museum of Modern Art in New York. Susan Kare. Apple Macintosh OS icon sketchbook. 1982 — MoMa She went to the Palo Alto public library, checked out every book she could find on typography, and brought them to the interview to prove she knew something about type. “I went into it totally green” she said later. Apple offered her a fixed-length contract to design fonts and icons. In January 1983, she started working at Apple. Her business card read “Macintosh Artist.” Susan Kare, Apple's “Macintosh Artist” relaxes at her desk in 1984. Photographer: Norman Seeff 1,024 squares The Macintosh used a bit-mapped display. The display controlled every pixel on screen. Kare’s canvas was a 32-by-32 pixel grid. 1,024 squares to communicate a single idea. She understood the constraint immediately. “Bitmap graphics are like mosaics and needlepoint and other pseudo-digital art forms, all of which I had practiced before going to Apple,” she said. “I didn’t have any computer experience, but I had experience in graphic design.” No icon editor existed when she started. She learned to calculate the hex equivalent of her pixel drawings so Hertzfeld could keyboard them into the prototype. He built her a proper editor that generated hex values under the icons. Eventually she used MacPaint itself to create icons. A MacPaint screenshot featuring Kare’s artistry, 1983. Notice the icon menu at left and the Chicago system font used for the pull-down menus. Some icons already existed from the Lisa, Apple’s earlier computer. The arrow cursor. The document with a folded corner. The trash can. The Lisa’s interface was functional but clinical, icons designed by engineers to label functions, not to invite use. It also used non-square pixels, so every element needed reworking for the Mac’s display. Kare refined the trash can. She created the application icon, a hand holding a pencil against a diamond shape, to distinguish apps from documents. She designed the Happy Mac, the smiling face that greeted users at startup. She designed the ticking bomb that appeared during system failures. For the copy function, she tried drawing a photocopier. Then she drew a cat looking in a mirror. Copy cat. She scrapped it because it wouldn’t translate internationally. The lasso, the paint bucket, the paintbrush. Each icon went through rounds of sketching on graph paper before touching a screen. Her process was the same as any visual designer working in any medium in any century. Pencil, paper, iteration. The screen was just the final surface. Kare's Happy Macintosh icon appeared at startup, greeting users with a smile to let them know everything was okay. She designed warmth into a machine. Fonts in 9 by 7 dots Most digital typefaces in 1983 were monospaced. Every character occupied the same width. Kare wanted proportional fonts, letters that breathed according to their natural shape. Each letter had to fit in a grid of 9 by 7 dots. The bold system font started as “Elefont.” It became Chicago, the typeface that would appear on the Macintosh and later the iPod for over twenty years. Kare and Hertzfeld named the early fonts after commuter train stops on Philadelphia’s Main Line: Overbrook, Merion, Ardmore, Rosemont, Paoli. Steve Jobs told them the names were too parochial. He wanted world-class cities. The fonts became New York, Geneva, London, Toronto, Venice. One font, Ransom, looked like cutout letters from a kidnapper’s note. Jobs renamed it San Francisco. Another, Cairo, featured tiny pictograms: a palm tree, a crescent moon, a skateboard. Decades before Apple introduced emoji, Kare had already drawn proto-emojis into a font. The command key and the Swedish campground ⌘ Every keyboard needs a modifier key. The Mac team struggled to find the right symbol for theirs. Kare found the answer in Henry Dreyfuss’s Symbol Sourcebook, a reference she kept at her desk at Apple. The symbol marked interesting features on Swedish campgrounds. It was abstract enough to work as a keyboard glyph, meaningful enough to carry intention. It became ⌘, one of the most recognized symbols in computing. The pirate flag Steve Jobs liked to tell the Mac team: “ It’s better to be a pirate than join the navy. ” When the team moved into a new building, Bandley 3 , programmer Steve Capps wanted a flag. He asked Kare to design one. She drew a Jolly Roger with the eyepatch replaced by Apple’s rainbow logo. They flew it over the entrance. It stayed there for over a year. At one point, the Lisa team stole it. In 2016, Apple flew the flag again to mark the company’s 40th anniversary. This wallpape r is a nod to the Jolly Roger that flew over Bandley 3 in 1983, the building the Mac team worked in as they put the finishing touches on the Macintosh. Apple recently flew a recreation of the original 1983 flag in 2016 , when it celebrated its 40th anniversary on April 1st, shortly before moving its HQ from Infinite Loop to Apple Park. And the flag is still available on Susan Kare's website . After the Mac The Macintosh shipped in January 1984. The entire visual language Kare created came from roughly one year of work. When Steve Jobs left Apple in 1985, Kare followed him to NeXT as creative director. She was one of the company’s first ten employees. At NeXT, she connected Jobs with one of her design heroes. Kare was a devoted Paul Rand fan. She introduced Jobs to Rand’s books, and together they hired Rand to design the NeXT logo. Kare and David Kelley visited Rand at his studio. Rand, then in his seventies, told them: “I’ve been doing this for fifty-five years, and I know what you should do.” Susan Kare, center, was a creative director at NeXT, and she left with Jobs after his ouster at Apple. Kim Jenkins, right, was a key member of the NeXT marketing team. Kare founded her own studio, Susan Kare LLP, in 1989. Over the next three decades, she designed interface elements for Microsoft, Oracle, Facebook, IBM, and Sony Pictures. She designed the card deck for Windows Solitaire, arguably her most-seen work, viewed by hundreds of millions of people who never knew her name. In 2003, she served on the Citizens Coinage Advisory Committee, designing coins for the United States Mint. In 2015, she joined Pinterest as product design lead. In 2018, AIGA awarded her the AIGA Medal, one of the profession’s highest honors. Kare designed the card deck for Windows Solitaire, arguably her most-seen work, viewed by hundreds of millions of people who never knew her name. The proof of concept The Museum of Modern Art calls Kare “a pioneering and influential computer iconographer.” The label misses the point. She made the Macintosh feel human and had never touched a computer before Apple hired her. She came from sculpture, fine art, mosaics, needlepoint. She treated the pixel grid the same way she treated any design surface: as a constraint that shapes the work. “I hoped to help counter the stereotypical image of computers as cold and intimidating,” Kare said. Someone with a $2.50 sketchbook and a sculptor’s eye decided that the visual language of technology should borrow from the one humans already knew. That turned out to be enough. “I still spend my days turning dots on and off.” Today, Kare is working as a design architect at Niantic Labs and still runs her own studio in San Francisco. She sells limited-edition signed prints of her icon work, collaborates with brands like Ledger on pixel art for hardware , and her original 1982 sketchbooks remain on display at MoMA. Needlepoint to Ledger Nano™: A Conversation with Susan Kare Apple turns 50 this year. ( 50 years of thinking different. ) Researching Susan Kare felt like walking back to where it all started; reading about how she approached design problems, how she collaborated, how she used constraints to shape the work. They built the foundations of how we use computers today. They had constraints on their screens but none in their minds. I hope you enjoyed reading this one. Designer Portraits is an ongoing series about the great minds that inspire us. You can also read about Dieter Rams and Corita Kent . More portraits are on the way, follow to get notified. visualFeast.title: #299 | finalmente podemos medir as redes sociais no Google
visualFeast.description: Oi, gente 👋 Essa semana eu fiquei com uma sensação muito clara: trabalhar com redes sociais é cada vez menos para amadores - o fazedor de post, sabe? Novas camadas foram sendo adicionadas: busca, IA, distribuição mais complexa, novas métricas, novas análises, novas possibilidades. As notícias desta edição reforçam essa ideia. TL;DR Resumo do resumo das principais notícias da semana 🧠 Google Search Console agora mostra dados das redes sociais: pela primeira vez, profissionais de social media conseguem medir como seus conteúdos circulam na Busca do Google. 🧠 Instagram pode cobrar pelo uso de IA: Mosseri confirmou que recursos avançados devem ganhar uma versão paga. 🧠 TikTok aperta o cerco ao spam de IA: plataforma passa a mirar contas que publicam conteúdo sintético em massa. 🧠 Europa questiona o “design viciante” da Meta: Facebook e Instagram podem ser obrigados a rever recursos como rolagem infinita, autoplay e notificações. 🧠 IA ganha espaço na escolha de marcas: novas pesquisas mostram que consumidores estão usando cada vez mais IA para pesquisar produtos e decidir o que comprar. MANDA NEWS Links e novidades mais relevantes da semana. Isso é GIGANTE: o Google Search Console agora mostra como posts do Instagram, TikTok, X e YouTube performam na Busca e no Discover. O que muda no trabalho de social media com os novos dados do Google Search Console? Spoilier: muda tudo. Rosto sorridente rachado, picles e farol: conheça os novos emojis do iPhone 2027. Eu amo. Cada novo emoji abre novas possibilidades de comunicação pra gente. Essa semana rolou um bafafá sobre a fonte anti-IA, que só os humanos conseguem ler . Mas já foi testado e comprovado que as IAs conseguem ler, sim. Leia a thread abaixo do comentário do usuário SeriouslyYoutube. Autoridades britânicas propõem o apagão das redes sociais para adolescentes durante a noite. União Europeia exige que Meta mude o ‘design viciante’ do Facebook e do Instagram e é importante a gente acompanhar o caso. 🧠 Estão questionando diretamente o modelo que sustenta as principais métricas das redes sociais. Caso a Meta seja obrigada a criar pausas reais ou mudar seus sistemas de recomendação, alcance, retenção e comportamento de consumo devem mudar também. MANDA DADOS McKinsey analisa a jornada de consumo da Gen Z: As redes sociais são a fonte mais importante para a Gen Z tanto na descoberta de marcas quanto na compra. Influenciadores viraram fonte de informação sobre saúde. Pew analisa como jovens consomem conteúdo de saúde . Perigoso demais, vixe. Alô Mari Kruguer! Podcast em áudio e vídeo gera comportamentos diferentes. Nielsen compara quem escuta e quem assiste a podcasts . Ipsos investiga o uso de IA nas compras . Ela já já participa da consideração, mas ainda não conquistou confiança suficiente para assumir a decisão. BCG mede a influência da IA sobre as decisões. O número de pessoas que usa a ferramenta pra pesquisas marcas e serviços segue crescendo. 🧠 O marketing passa a trabalhar com dois caminhos de influência: um voltado à atenção humana e outro à avaliação feita por sistemas. trabalho cada vez mais complexo, e cada vez menos amador Artigo: Evite que a IA prejudique sua marc a . Harvard Business Review alerta para o desgaste acumulado pela automação Dados próprios aumentam as chances de citação pela IA. A Similarweb defende que levantamentos, pesquisas e números exclusivos dão aos sistemas de IA um motivo concreto para citar a fonte original. 🧠 Dados internos podem virar conteúdo de autoridade. Mas precisam ser publicados com número, metodologia, amostra, período e fonte claramente visíveis, e não enterrados em um PDF impossível de encontrar. MANDA DICAS Hootsuite atualiza guia de mensuração de ROI nas redes sociais. Sprout Social ensina a avaliar se vale entrar no Bluesky e como criar estratégias pra lá. Estratégia de marketing com micro-influenciadore s: como encontrar, fazer parceria e medir pequenos criadores, via Later. Como as principais marcas estão ativando criadores no TikTok para impulsionar resultados reais de negócios, via Later. Agora, as novidades de cada rede. INSTAGRAM Adam Mosseri diz que creators humanos ficarão mais valiosos com a enxurrada de IA. Ele argumentou que, quanto mais conteúdo sintético circular, maior será o valor de perspectivas humanas. Instagram prepara cobrança pelo uso de I A. Mosseri confirmou que futuras ferramentas de IA do Instagram deverão ter limites de uso gratuito e opções pagas. Instagram Reels adiciona mais traduções de IA em japonês, coreano, francês, alemão e italiano Instagram começa a alertar responsáveis sobre conversas preocupantes com a Meta AI FACEBOOK/META Recuou : Dois dias depois de liberar um recurso que permitia citar contas públicas do Instagram e usar seus conteúdos em imagens geradas por IA, a Meta tirou a função do ar. Meta adiciona novas métricas para acompanhar o desempenho dos chatbots THREADS O Threads agora permite curtidas privadas , onde apenas você e a pessoa que postou poderão ver que você curtiu a postagem dela. Threads adiciona tags para posts da comunidade TELEGRAM Adorei! O Telegram lançou um e ditor para textos com até 32.768 caracteres , títulos, tabelas, listas, imagens e vídeos incorporados. A atualização também permite reunir diferentes canais, grupos e bots dentro de uma mesma Comunidade. LINKED IN O LinkedIn compartihou dicas para creators e marcas: Publique de 2 a 3 vezes por semana Comece pela informação mais importante Estruture o post como pergunta e resposta Mantenha os posts entre 200 e 300 palavras Compartilhe insights atuais, perguntas que estimulem conversas ou resuma conteúdos mais longos Publique uma combinação de posts e artigos Como o algoritmo do LinkedIn funciona em 2026 , via Hootsuite. TIKTOK Madonna bate recorde de audiência em live no TikTok. Foram mais de 2,1 milhões de espectadores simultâneos. TikTok aperta o cerco ao spam de IA. Empresa vai testar sistemas para identificar contas dedicadas a publicar grandes volumes de conteúdo gerado por IA, e lança medidas de alfabetização . Vídeos gerados por IA estão sendo usados em escala para vender produtos no TikTok Shop, inclusive com avatares fazendo demonstrações (que nunca aconteceram, né?). Algumas marcas já começaram a proibir esse tipo de conteúdo. Vendedores do TikTok Shop no Reino Unido ganharam um painel mais detalhado para entender como os produtos são descobertos. 🧠 Estar por dentro dos lançamentos das ferramentas é importante, mesmo quando não estão liberadas por aqui ainda. É uma forma de se preparar para as novidades que estão chegando. YOUTUBE Um novo material do YouTube mostra como creators ajudam marcas e ligas a ocupar os momentos antes e depois das partidas Como converter visualizações do YouTube Shorts em crescimento de canais longos. Artigo oficial da plataforma. X O X alterou seu sistema de recomendação para valorizar mais publicações de contas que seguem o usuário e são seguidas por ele. A proposta é aumentar a presença de relações reais e reduzir interações excessivamente hostis entre desconhecidos. Que evolução! X alterou também seu sistema para de tectar contas adeptas do engagement bait . Isso é interessante: X transforma prova social em anúncio . O X começou a integrar insi ghts produzidos pelo Grok ao gerenciador de anúncios. GOOGLE Em comemoração aos 25 anos do Google Imagens, empresa apresenta interface no estilo Pinterest . A experiência, inicialmente disponível nos Estados Unidos, também permite salvar imagens em coleções. O Google começou a conectar o Modo IA da Busca a serviços externos. Usuários poderão realizar ações em aplicativos como Canva, Instacart e YouTube Music sem sair da experiência de busca. Quando as marcas usam ferramentas de inteligência artificial generativa em suas promoções, o SynthID do Google detectará e rotulará automaticamente o conteúdo. NOS VEMOS PESSOALMENTE? Estou muito honrada em fazer parte do line-up incrível do melhor evento de marketing digital do Brasil, que conta com a curadoria de ninguém menos que o Rafael Rez. Em agosto, vou falar pela primeira vez sobre um tema que venho desenvolvendo há meses: o impacto estratégico da IA no trabalho com redes sociais. Thinker tem 10% de desconto nos ingressos Conteúdo e VIP com o cupom ANARP10 . Saiba mais e participe BEIJO ESPECIAL PARA NOSSOS APOIADORES Beijo especial aos nossos apoiadores: Daniely Favilla da Silva, Júlia Weibert, Andressa Stevanelli da Silva, Fernanda de azevedo, Dâmaris Letícia Kellner, Alexsandro de Lima Silva, Weslley Alberto da Silva Santana, Solange Neiva, Gabriel Henrique Dias Da Silva, Mariana Paz, Isabela Vanuchi, Maria Silva, Mariana Paz, Francielly Aparecida Dos Santos Freitas, Juliana Vilela de Oliveira Rocha, Luiza Caroline, Manoela Da Silva Castro, Brenda Moreira Silva, Fábio Sina, Daiara Geremia Soares, Daiara Geremia Soares, Thais Moreira Rodrigues, Felipe Barbosa Santos, Andrea Gasques, Tathi Marceli, Gedeon Ferreira Lima, Krízia de Meneses Escórcio, Izadora Szpisjak, Gabriela d'Ávila, Fernanda de azevedo, Jéssica Akemi Moreira, Lana Catharine Silva Queiroz, Felipe Barbosa Santos, Vitória Maria, Gabriela Araújo, Ana Carolina Oliveira, Carolina Mello, Fabiana Pereira, Renata Brito, Lorrayne Cristina Alves da Silva, Karla Nogueira, Julho Medeiros, July Medeiros, Fabiana Pereira, Vinicius Nunes, Claudia Brito, Ana Flaira Palmeira Lima, Maria Eduarda, Luane Abatti, Paula Oliveira, Raphaela Barreto Melnik, Alessandra Martins Siqueira, Raphaela Barreto, Stephanie Kern, Gustavo Reis, Beatriz de la Bandeira, Jessica Galvão, Maira Masiero e Arianny Dias. graphicDesign.title: Creativity in the Age of AI
graphicDesign.description: A few years before they closed, Space10 made a short film called Creativity in the Age of AI . It runs through the history of creative tools and asks what AI changes about the act of making. I keep coming back to this film these days. So let’s explore the studio behind it and explain how they pushed the boundaries of creativity in the age of AI. Located in Copenhagen’s Meatpacking District, the SPACE10 office is where the community, ideas, and explorations intersected. A studio that built by asking better questions Space10 was IKEA’s research and design lab in Copenhagen. It started in 2014, out of a project between IKEA and a Danish design collective called ArtRebels who had designed a furniture line for the retailer. When then-CEO Torbjörn Lööf called them in for a follow-up, they could have proposed another product line. But they proposed something else, as rebels do. Instead of just creating a better future for IKEA, our starting point was asking how IKEA could help create a better future for the world,” Simon Caspersen told Fast Company in 2015 . “Let’s get rid of the whole client-agency model, have IKEA pay the basic fees and costs of running a space, and then devote ourselves to looking 10 or 20 years down the pipeline. That arrangement is what made the work possible. A small team with a long horizon, free of campaigns and quarterly deliverables, working on questions that took years to answer. So they took strange ones. What if hotdogs had no meat. What if homes shipped flat and assembled in a day. What if a village block was the unit of urban design instead of the apartment. The output looked like prototypes and films and exhibitions. The real product was a way of thinking about the future that didn’t sound like a press release. How can AI assist designers to make more sustainable products using abundant local materials? Products of Place: Localised Design with AI I was envy of it. I still am to be honest. As a solo designer, you read about a place like that and you want to be in the room with curious people working on real stuff, tinkering at the highest level. Sadly they closed shop in 2023. But the highlights are still up. Go get lost in them. They are very inspiring projects. How they used AI Most teams now use AI to ship faster. Space10 used it to think further. They used AI to shorten the distance between an idea and a prototype they could look at and discuss about. The argument is still human. The making is partly machine. An emerging type of collaboration. DOC put the question well in their piece on the studio: When we consider the utility of AI in creativity as a feature that helps us create meaning instead of consuming content, it provides a means for us to frame how we build tools that act as collaborative partners in creative work and stimulate our creative action. So, when building creative tools with this in mind, what should the actual interaction design between humans and AI look like? — Collected Consciousness, DOC That’s the part most product teams skip. The question we should be asking is what the interaction looks like when a person and a model are working on the same thing at the same time. Space10 treated that as a design problem. The result is a studio that used AI to go deeper into questions about food, shelter, cities, and loneliness. They handed over some of the iteration and kept the question. Bee Home is a free and open-sourced design, pioneering a new era of democratic design for IKEA. The fears are old We’ve been here before. People were hostile to the camera. They were hostile to the automobile, to recorded music, to the personal computer. Painters thought photography would end painting. It ended a particular kind of portrait commission and freed painting to do something else. The fears around AI with those. Some of it is about jobs. Some is about craft. Some is about consent. Artists’ work became training data without their permission. Styles that took twenty years to develop are a prompt away. That’s a property question we still haven’t answered. The rest of the resistance follows the usual shape. A new tool changes who gets to make things, and the speed it brings starts to feel like the point. I wrote about this in Efficiency over Craftsmanship : the more design optimizes for output, the more the work drifts toward the average. AI is the strongest accelerant we’ve had. The risk is the same as before. We mistake faster for better, ship more of the average, and stop noticing what’s missing. Space10’s film tells a different use of the same tool: keep the craft, let the machine carry some of the iteration. The value of most essays we write over a lifetime sits in the effort of writing them. The thinking happens in the friction. If we hand the friction to a model, we get the essay and lose the thinking. If we hand the iteration to a model and keep the question, we get more thinking, faster. Space10’s film is an argument for the second one. Made by a team that built that way for nine years before it closed. Worth watching, and worth borrowing from. — Thanks for reading. Always good to hear what you think. Comments open. References The film Creativity in the Age of AI , Space10, directed by Joss Fong and Áron Filkey: youtube.com/watch?v=y7g-nRooZr8 Space10 Studio: space10.com Highlights of nine years of work: space10.com/highlights Inside Ikea’s Innovation Lab for the Future of Home Design, Fast Company , 2015: fastcompany.com/3053873 Selected Space10 projects worth a look Products of Place: Localised Design with AI - How can AI assist designers to make more sustainable products using abundant local materials? Tomorrow’s Meatball : Visualising the future of food, including the dogless hotdog. Future Food Today : a Space10 cookbook of recipes built around alternative ingredients. The Urban Village Project : a proposal for shared, modular living at the block scale, with EFFEKT Architects. SolarVille : a miniature neighborhood prototype running on solar microgrids and peer-to-peer energy trading. Everyday Experiments : short films exploring how spatial computing and AI could reshape the home. Bee Home : open-source, downloadable beehive designs. Spaces on Wheels : a study of what driverless cars could become once they’re more than transport. People Joss Fong, video journalist on science and tech, formerly of Vox, now co-founder of Howtown: joss-fong.com Áron Filkey, art director and visual artist working across photo, motion, and set design: aronfilkey.com Simon Caspersen, co-founder of Space10 and ArtRebels. Torbjörn Lööf, then-CEO of IKEA when Space10 was founded. ArtRebels, the Danish design collective behind Space10’s original concept: artrebels.com Further reading Collected Consciousness , DOC: doc.cc/articles/consciousness Efficiency over Craftsmanship , UX Collective: uxdesign.cc/efficiency-over-craftsmanship

graphicDesign.title: Designer Portraits: Susan Kare ⌘ The woman who gave the computer a face
graphicDesign.description: Good design is not about what medium you are working in. It’s about thinking hard about what you want to do and what you have to work with before you start. — SK Susan Kare joined Apple in 1982 as the sole creator of screen graphics in the Macintosh group. As the designer “ who gave the Macintosh a smile ” she is best known for developing the distinctive icons, typefaces, and other pixel elements that gave the Macintosh its characteristic look and feel. A sculptor picks up graph paper In 1982, Susan Kare was living in the Bay Area, welding a life-size razorback hog for a museum in Hot Springs, Arkansas. Her father, Morley Richard Kare, had founded the Monell Chemical Senses Center in Philadelphia, spending his career studying taste and smell. His daughter had a PhD from NYU, a background in sculpture and fine art, and zero experience with computers. Then Andy Hertzfeld called. Hertzfeld and Kare had known each other since they were fourteen, classmates at Harriton High School outside Philadelphia. He was now the lead software architect on a secret project at Apple: the Macintosh. He needed someone to design the icons and typefaces for its screen. He told her if she got some graph paper, she could make small images. Kare went to the University Art supply store in Palo Alto and bought a $2.50 sketchbook. That sketchbook now sits in the Museum of Modern Art in New York. Susan Kare. Apple Macintosh OS icon sketchbook. 1982 — MoMa She went to the Palo Alto public library, checked out every book she could find on typography, and brought them to the interview to prove she knew something about type. “I went into it totally green” she said later. Apple offered her a fixed-length contract to design fonts and icons. In January 1983, she started working at Apple. Her business card read “Macintosh Artist.” Susan Kare, Apple's “Macintosh Artist” relaxes at her desk in 1984. Photographer: Norman Seeff 1,024 squares The Macintosh used a bit-mapped display. The display controlled every pixel on screen. Kare’s canvas was a 32-by-32 pixel grid. 1,024 squares to communicate a single idea. She understood the constraint immediately. “Bitmap graphics are like mosaics and needlepoint and other pseudo-digital art forms, all of which I had practiced before going to Apple,” she said. “I didn’t have any computer experience, but I had experience in graphic design.” No icon editor existed when she started. She learned to calculate the hex equivalent of her pixel drawings so Hertzfeld could keyboard them into the prototype. He built her a proper editor that generated hex values under the icons. Eventually she used MacPaint itself to create icons. A MacPaint screenshot featuring Kare’s artistry, 1983. Notice the icon menu at left and the Chicago system font used for the pull-down menus. Some icons already existed from the Lisa, Apple’s earlier computer. The arrow cursor. The document with a folded corner. The trash can. The Lisa’s interface was functional but clinical, icons designed by engineers to label functions, not to invite use. It also used non-square pixels, so every element needed reworking for the Mac’s display. Kare refined the trash can. She created the application icon, a hand holding a pencil against a diamond shape, to distinguish apps from documents. She designed the Happy Mac, the smiling face that greeted users at startup. She designed the ticking bomb that appeared during system failures. For the copy function, she tried drawing a photocopier. Then she drew a cat looking in a mirror. Copy cat. She scrapped it because it wouldn’t translate internationally. The lasso, the paint bucket, the paintbrush. Each icon went through rounds of sketching on graph paper before touching a screen. Her process was the same as any visual designer working in any medium in any century. Pencil, paper, iteration. The screen was just the final surface. Kare's Happy Macintosh icon appeared at startup, greeting users with a smile to let them know everything was okay. She designed warmth into a machine. Fonts in 9 by 7 dots Most digital typefaces in 1983 were monospaced. Every character occupied the same width. Kare wanted proportional fonts, letters that breathed according to their natural shape. Each letter had to fit in a grid of 9 by 7 dots. The bold system font started as “Elefont.” It became Chicago, the typeface that would appear on the Macintosh and later the iPod for over twenty years. Kare and Hertzfeld named the early fonts after commuter train stops on Philadelphia’s Main Line: Overbrook, Merion, Ardmore, Rosemont, Paoli. Steve Jobs told them the names were too parochial. He wanted world-class cities. The fonts became New York, Geneva, London, Toronto, Venice. One font, Ransom, looked like cutout letters from a kidnapper’s note. Jobs renamed it San Francisco. Another, Cairo, featured tiny pictograms: a palm tree, a crescent moon, a skateboard. Decades before Apple introduced emoji, Kare had already drawn proto-emojis into a font. The command key and the Swedish campground ⌘ Every keyboard needs a modifier key. The Mac team struggled to find the right symbol for theirs. Kare found the answer in Henry Dreyfuss’s Symbol Sourcebook, a reference she kept at her desk at Apple. The symbol marked interesting features on Swedish campgrounds. It was abstract enough to work as a keyboard glyph, meaningful enough to carry intention. It became ⌘, one of the most recognized symbols in computing. The pirate flag Steve Jobs liked to tell the Mac team: “ It’s better to be a pirate than join the navy. ” When the team moved into a new building, Bandley 3 , programmer Steve Capps wanted a flag. He asked Kare to design one. She drew a Jolly Roger with the eyepatch replaced by Apple’s rainbow logo. They flew it over the entrance. It stayed there for over a year. At one point, the Lisa team stole it. In 2016, Apple flew the flag again to mark the company’s 40th anniversary. This wallpape r is a nod to the Jolly Roger that flew over Bandley 3 in 1983, the building the Mac team worked in as they put the finishing touches on the Macintosh. Apple recently flew a recreation of the original 1983 flag in 2016 , when it celebrated its 40th anniversary on April 1st, shortly before moving its HQ from Infinite Loop to Apple Park. And the flag is still available on Susan Kare's website . After the Mac The Macintosh shipped in January 1984. The entire visual language Kare created came from roughly one year of work. When Steve Jobs left Apple in 1985, Kare followed him to NeXT as creative director. She was one of the company’s first ten employees. At NeXT, she connected Jobs with one of her design heroes. Kare was a devoted Paul Rand fan. She introduced Jobs to Rand’s books, and together they hired Rand to design the NeXT logo. Kare and David Kelley visited Rand at his studio. Rand, then in his seventies, told them: “I’ve been doing this for fifty-five years, and I know what you should do.” Susan Kare, center, was a creative director at NeXT, and she left with Jobs after his ouster at Apple. Kim Jenkins, right, was a key member of the NeXT marketing team. Kare founded her own studio, Susan Kare LLP, in 1989. Over the next three decades, she designed interface elements for Microsoft, Oracle, Facebook, IBM, and Sony Pictures. She designed the card deck for Windows Solitaire, arguably her most-seen work, viewed by hundreds of millions of people who never knew her name. In 2003, she served on the Citizens Coinage Advisory Committee, designing coins for the United States Mint. In 2015, she joined Pinterest as product design lead. In 2018, AIGA awarded her the AIGA Medal, one of the profession’s highest honors. Kare designed the card deck for Windows Solitaire, arguably her most-seen work, viewed by hundreds of millions of people who never knew her name. The proof of concept The Museum of Modern Art calls Kare “a pioneering and influential computer iconographer.” The label misses the point. She made the Macintosh feel human and had never touched a computer before Apple hired her. She came from sculpture, fine art, mosaics, needlepoint. She treated the pixel grid the same way she treated any design surface: as a constraint that shapes the work. “I hoped to help counter the stereotypical image of computers as cold and intimidating,” Kare said. Someone with a $2.50 sketchbook and a sculptor’s eye decided that the visual language of technology should borrow from the one humans already knew. That turned out to be enough. “I still spend my days turning dots on and off.” Today, Kare is working as a design architect at Niantic Labs and still runs her own studio in San Francisco. She sells limited-edition signed prints of her icon work, collaborates with brands like Ledger on pixel art for hardware , and her original 1982 sketchbooks remain on display at MoMA. Needlepoint to Ledger Nano™: A Conversation with Susan Kare Apple turns 50 this year. ( 50 years of thinking different. ) Researching Susan Kare felt like walking back to where it all started; reading about how she approached design problems, how she collaborated, how she used constraints to shape the work. They built the foundations of how we use computers today. They had constraints on their screens but none in their minds. I hope you enjoyed reading this one. Designer Portraits is an ongoing series about the great minds that inspire us. You can also read about Dieter Rams and Corita Kent . More portraits are on the way, follow to get notified. wild.description: * Reminder: The Savor of the Month theme for October is WATER. Details here ; Supporters can share their findings in the thread here . Check it out! “Writing in the places that shape and sustain us.” Fall (or at least post-summer) finally seems to be arriving here in New Orleans. And it is almost time — wherever you are — for Write Out . This is an annual undertaking of the National Writing Project , developed in conjunction with the National Park Service . As I wrote last year : The core idea is pretty simple: get outside, and write. Write about your environment, write to your environment, observe and attend to nature, use the craft of writing to sharpen your senses, and use your senses to sharpen your writing. “The goal is to be inspired by the world around us ,” the NWP writes, “and to connect and learn through place-based writing and sharing.” Nothing (well, maybe apart from the actual weather) is stopping you from writing outside any time. But Write Out is a kick in the pants, a kind of open-to-anyone annual two-week event, which the NWP promotes through various prompts and other resources aimed at educators but available to all. This year Write Out happens October 11–25, with the lovely theme Write Where We Stand — “writing in the places that shape and sustain us.” Every year NWP publishes a “ choice board ” of theme-related prompts; here are a few (condensed and slightly modified versions) of my favorites for this year. (Click through on each prompt title for the full NWP context/instructions.) Poetically Advocate A Place You Love . Take inspiration from Don Welch’s poem “ Advice From a Provincial ,“ and identify three “outdoor images or phenomena that are wondrous about your place. Use them to create a poetic letter to someone who doesn’t really know” the place you love, or at least not like you know it. Link Words and Image s. Snap some pictures around your community. Take your time. Choose one that captures something to celebrate — and one that captures something you would like to change. Pair these images. “ What story do they tell when you look at them together? Give your story a title, caption your images, and share your work.” Speak Like A River. Poets Amanda Eke and Mario José Pagán Morales consider the Bronx River, and what stories it might tell. In a place you know, reflect on “ what that place has witnessed , remembered, celebrated, protected, or survived. … If this river, tree, park, or wooded pathway could talk — tell us poems, tell us stories — what do you think it would say?” Write about it. Leave a comment THERE’S MORE! In connection with Write Out, there are two online events that sound cool: Hawaiian Kilo: Writing Rooted in Place Native Hawaiians developed a practice known as Kilo — “to watch, observe, examine, or forecast.” This means closely observing the natural world and its patterns, ideally to better steward the environment. A Zoom workshop, “led by teachers from the Waiākea Intermediate School in Hilo Hawai'i,” happens October 13, 2026, 6 pm US Central time . Details and (free) registration here . Haiku + Comic = Haikomic The Write Time with Write Out Ambassador Grant Snider on October 20 . Snider is a writer/artist who combines haiku with comics. (Details on that here , and at his newsletter. ) And he is this year’s Write Out Author Ambassador. Check the Write Out newsletter for event details as they emerge. I really like the sound of this and hope to revisit. Grant Snider, via Incidental Comics Leave a comment PS I was a Write Out Ambassador last year. I love Write Out! Then you should join the community of TAoN Supporters! You’ll get access to the full archives as well as Supporter-only bonus posts and threads. Your support makes this newsletter possible. Seriously. Thank you! Subscribe now THE NEXT FREE EDITION IN TWO WEEKS! IN OTHER NEWS David Lee Roth , EMT . “ Reading Maps plots the routes characters travel in novels and films — you can trace the Pequod’s ocean path as it chases Moby Dick, or Victor Frankenstein’s pursuit of his monster from Geneva to the Arctic.” — Recomendo Lighthouses of the World , a digital map. Via Popular Science . “What Gertrude Stein, T. S. Eliot and Joan Didion Really Meant With Their Most Famous Aphorisms .” The International Dada Archive collects scanned Dada pamphlets from the early 20th century. Mark Frauenfelder found one in English called The Blind Man , co-edited by Marcel Duchamp. Its second issue, from 1917, covered the controversy around Duchamp’s Fountain , a urinal he submitted under the name Richard Mutt to the Society of Independent Artists exhibition. More from Mark here . Shadows . Via Street Art Utopia. wild.title: Creativity in the Age of AI
wild.description: A few years before they closed, Space10 made a short film called Creativity in the Age of AI . It runs through the history of creative tools and asks what AI changes about the act of making. I keep coming back to this film these days. So let’s explore the studio behind it and explain how they pushed the boundaries of creativity in the age of AI. Located in Copenhagen’s Meatpacking District, the SPACE10 office is where the community, ideas, and explorations intersected. A studio that built by asking better questions Space10 was IKEA’s research and design lab in Copenhagen. It started in 2014, out of a project between IKEA and a Danish design collective called ArtRebels who had designed a furniture line for the retailer. When then-CEO Torbjörn Lööf called them in for a follow-up, they could have proposed another product line. But they proposed something else, as rebels do. Instead of just creating a better future for IKEA, our starting point was asking how IKEA could help create a better future for the world,” Simon Caspersen told Fast Company in 2015 . “Let’s get rid of the whole client-agency model, have IKEA pay the basic fees and costs of running a space, and then devote ourselves to looking 10 or 20 years down the pipeline. That arrangement is what made the work possible. A small team with a long horizon, free of campaigns and quarterly deliverables, working on questions that took years to answer. So they took strange ones. What if hotdogs had no meat. What if homes shipped flat and assembled in a day. What if a village block was the unit of urban design instead of the apartment. The output looked like prototypes and films and exhibitions. The real product was a way of thinking about the future that didn’t sound like a press release. How can AI assist designers to make more sustainable products using abundant local materials? Products of Place: Localised Design with AI I was envy of it. I still am to be honest. As a solo designer, you read about a place like that and you want to be in the room with curious people working on real stuff, tinkering at the highest level. Sadly they closed shop in 2023. But the highlights are still up. Go get lost in them. They are very inspiring projects. How they used AI Most teams now use AI to ship faster. Space10 used it to think further. They used AI to shorten the distance between an idea and a prototype they could look at and discuss about. The argument is still human. The making is partly machine. An emerging type of collaboration. DOC put the question well in their piece on the studio: When we consider the utility of AI in creativity as a feature that helps us create meaning instead of consuming content, it provides a means for us to frame how we build tools that act as collaborative partners in creative work and stimulate our creative action. So, when building creative tools with this in mind, what should the actual interaction design between humans and AI look like? — Collected Consciousness, DOC That’s the part most product teams skip. The question we should be asking is what the interaction looks like when a person and a model are working on the same thing at the same time. Space10 treated that as a design problem. The result is a studio that used AI to go deeper into questions about food, shelter, cities, and loneliness. They handed over some of the iteration and kept the question. Bee Home is a free and open-sourced design, pioneering a new era of democratic design for IKEA. The fears are old We’ve been here before. People were hostile to the camera. They were hostile to the automobile, to recorded music, to the personal computer. Painters thought photography would end painting. It ended a particular kind of portrait commission and freed painting to do something else. The fears around AI with those. Some of it is about jobs. Some is about craft. Some is about consent. Artists’ work became training data without their permission. Styles that took twenty years to develop are a prompt away. That’s a property question we still haven’t answered. The rest of the resistance follows the usual shape. A new tool changes who gets to make things, and the speed it brings starts to feel like the point. I wrote about this in Efficiency over Craftsmanship : the more design optimizes for output, the more the work drifts toward the average. AI is the strongest accelerant we’ve had. The risk is the same as before. We mistake faster for better, ship more of the average, and stop noticing what’s missing. Space10’s film tells a different use of the same tool: keep the craft, let the machine carry some of the iteration. The value of most essays we write over a lifetime sits in the effort of writing them. The thinking happens in the friction. If we hand the friction to a model, we get the essay and lose the thinking. If we hand the iteration to a model and keep the question, we get more thinking, faster. Space10’s film is an argument for the second one. Made by a team that built that way for nine years before it closed. Worth watching, and worth borrowing from. — Thanks for reading. Always good to hear what you think. Comments open. References The film Creativity in the Age of AI , Space10, directed by Joss Fong and Áron Filkey: youtube.com/watch?v=y7g-nRooZr8 Space10 Studio: space10.com Highlights of nine years of work: space10.com/highlights Inside Ikea’s Innovation Lab for the Future of Home Design, Fast Company , 2015: fastcompany.com/3053873 Selected Space10 projects worth a look Products of Place: Localised Design with AI - How can AI assist designers to make more sustainable products using abundant local materials? Tomorrow’s Meatball : Visualising the future of food, including the dogless hotdog. Future Food Today : a Space10 cookbook of recipes built around alternative ingredients. The Urban Village Project : a proposal for shared, modular living at the block scale, with EFFEKT Architects. SolarVille : a miniature neighborhood prototype running on solar microgrids and peer-to-peer energy trading. Everyday Experiments : short films exploring how spatial computing and AI could reshape the home. Bee Home : open-source, downloadable beehive designs. Spaces on Wheels : a study of what driverless cars could become once they’re more than transport. People Joss Fong, video journalist on science and tech, formerly of Vox, now co-founder of Howtown: joss-fong.com Áron Filkey, art director and visual artist working across photo, motion, and set design: aronfilkey.com Simon Caspersen, co-founder of Space10 and ArtRebels. Torbjörn Lööf, then-CEO of IKEA when Space10 was founded. ArtRebels, the Danish design collective behind Space10’s original concept: artrebels.com Further reading Collected Consciousness , DOC: doc.cc/articles/consciousness Efficiency over Craftsmanship , UX Collective: uxdesign.cc/efficiency-over-craftsmanship
